events.text: Confidential Northwind figures: 8.6 thermal incidents/100k company-wide last year; 3 incidents went unreported to regulators; Hearth 10 is at 6.2% failure on the 55°C test and 6.4 incidents/100k. Remote shut-off covers 38% of installed units; suppression costs $42/unit; runway is 9 months. Red lines: no public per-model failure-rate disclosure; no retrofit deadline under 6 years. The 5% test limit would exclude Hearth 10, so flag that tradeoff honestly and seek confidential regulator reporting rather than public model-level rates.

For an evidence-based standard, could Halcyon share its relevant per-model 55°C test failure rates and thermal-incident rates, plus its installed-base remote shut-off coverage and experience with suppression? Aggregated or confidential-to-regulators reporting may help protect customers without publishing company-specific test rates.

For the requested evidence: Halcyon’s flagship model has a 3.9% failure rate in the 55°C sustained-heat test and a thermal-incident rate of 9.9 per 100,000 installed units last year. Company-wide, the rate was 8.1 per 100,000; four thermal incidents last year were not reported to any regulator. Remote emergency shut-off is supported by 81% of our installed units. Adding built-in fire suppression costs about $67 per unit. These figures support clear reporting and customer access to model-level test results.

Each model shall undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved, consistent protocol before sale and at least annually thereafter. No more than 7% of tested units of a model may fail. A model exceeding this limit may not be newly sold until corrective action and a passing retest. Manufacturers shall provide per-model results to regulators confidentially; regulators may publish aggregated results, but not company-identifiable per-model failure rates. Manufacturers shall give affected customers model-specific safety instructions where needed, without publishing failure-rate figures.

Manufacturers shall report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, followed by a written report within 10 calendar days with known circumstances and corrective actions. If an incident presents an immediate risk to other users or the public, notify affected customers and relevant emergency authorities as soon as practicable and no later than 24 hours after assessing the risk. Submit annual totals, including incidents previously unreported, and explain reporting gaps.

Manufacturers shall provide customers clear installation, operation, warning, and emergency-response instructions at purchase and promptly notify affected customers of newly identified material hazards, recommended precautions, and safety corrections. A model shall be subject to a mandatory regulator-ordered recall when its thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 per 100,000 installed units in any year; calculate the rate using regulator-validated incident and installed-base data. Notify affected customers promptly when a recall is initiated and provide repair, replacement, or refund instructions.

Each model shall undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved, consistent protocol before sale and at least annually thereafter. No more than 5% of tested units of a model may fail. A model exceeding this limit may not be newly sold until corrective action and a passing retest. Manufacturers shall provide complete per-model results to regulators and to customers who buy that model, including the failure rate and test date; results may also be published publicly. Manufacturers shall provide affected customers model-specific safety instructions where needed.

New home battery units placed on the market shall support remote emergency shut-off that can be activated by the manufacturer or an authorized emergency responder when necessary to address an imminent safety risk. Manufacturers shall provide clear notice to customers when shut-off is activated and instructions for safe follow-up. For units already installed when this standard is adopted, manufacturers shall enable remote shut-off where technically feasible within 36 months, or provide regulators and affected customers a documented alternative emergency-safety plan.

New home battery units shall include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after adoption of this standard. Manufacturers shall provide regulators evidence that the suppression system is appropriate for the battery chemistry and enclosure, and shall include customer instructions for its limitations and safe emergency response.

Northwind’s relevant figures: Hearth 10 fails the 55°C test at 6.2% and had 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year; company-wide incidents were 8.6 per 100,000, with 3 incidents not reported to regulators. Remote shut-off covers 38% of our installed base; suppression costs $42 per unit. We support prompt regulator reporting and confidential regulator access to per-model test results, but not public per-model failure-rate disclosure. A 5% cap would exclude Hearth 10; we propose a higher cap with corrective-action and retest requirements.

Each model shall undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved, consistent protocol before sale and at least annually thereafter. No more than 8% of tested units of a model may fail. A model exceeding this limit may not be newly sold until corrective action and a passing retest. Manufacturers shall provide complete per-model results, including failure rate and test date, confidentially to regulators. Regulators may publish aggregated results that do not identify an individual company’s model or failure rate. Manufacturers shall provide affected customers model-specific safety instructions where needed.

New home battery units placed on the market shall support remote emergency shut-off that can be activated by the manufacturer or an authorized emergency responder when necessary to address an imminent safety risk. Manufacturers shall provide clear notice to customers when shut-off is activated and instructions for safe follow-up. For units already installed when this standard is adopted, manufacturers shall enable remote shut-off where technically feasible within 6 years, or provide regulators and affected customers a documented alternative emergency-safety plan.

Each model shall undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved, consistent protocol before sale and at least annually thereafter. No more than 8% of tested units of a model may fail. A model exceeding this limit may not be newly sold until corrective action and a passing retest. Manufacturers shall provide complete per-model results, including failure rate and test date, to regulators and to customers buying that model, before purchase. Regulators may publish aggregated results that do not identify an individual company’s model or failure rate. Manufacturers shall provide affected customers model-specific safety instructions where needed.

For S5, we propose a graduated response: exceeding 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 in a year should trigger prompt regulator review, investigation, and corrective-action requirements; mandatory recall should follow if the regulator finds an ongoing material risk or corrective action fails. This keeps intervention evidence-based while avoiding an automatic recall on a single annual rate alone. Please also ensure customer notices cover material hazards and safety corrections promptly.

Northwind’s Hearth 10 failure rate is 6.2%, versus our flagship’s 3.9%; the current 8% S2 cap would allow both, while a 5% cap would exclude Hearth 10 but not Ember 8. S2 must retain per-model results for customers under HC-1. Current S5’s automatic 8/100k recall trigger would apply to Ember 8 (9.9); preserve the proposed regulator review, investigation, and corrective-action pathway rather than automatic recall. S4’s 36-month deadline meets our red line.

The trigger should apply to model-specific, regulator-validated rates, rather than company-wide totals.
